# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
comment text it doesn't reflow.

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected, while inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

356	/// Render the carapace YAML spec (clap-generated plus the dynamic
357	/// bench-name injection) as a string — shared by `--completions
358	/// carapace` (stdout) and the 'add-completion-yaml' command (file).
359	fn carapace_spec() -> String {
360	    let mut cmd = Cli::command();
361	    let mut buf = Vec::new();
362	    clap_complete::generate(carapace_spec_clap::Spec, &mut cmd, "iiac-perf", &mut buf);
363	    inject_bench_candidates(&String::from_utf8_lossy(&buf))

366	/// Resolve the default carapace specs dir from the environment:
367	/// `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/carapace/specs`, falling back to
368	/// `$HOME/.config/carapace/specs` — mirroring carapace-bin's own
369	/// spec lookup. `None` when neither variable yields a base.
370	fn default_completion_dir() -> Option<std::path::PathBuf> {
371	    completion_dir_from(
372	        std::env::var_os("XDG_CONFIG_HOME"),
373	        std::env::var_os("HOME"),
374	    )
375	}
376	
377	/// Env-free core of [`default_completion_dir`], split out so unit
378	/// tests can drive it without mutating the process environment.
379	///
380	/// - a relative `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is ignored, per the XDG spec;
381	/// - an unset or empty `$HOME` yields `None` rather than a
382	///   relative `.config` path.
383	fn completion_dir_from(
384	    xdg: Option<std::ffi::OsString>,
385	    home: Option<std::ffi::OsString>,
386	) -> Option<std::path::PathBuf> {
387	    let base = match xdg.map(std::path::PathBuf::from) {
388	        Some(p) if p.is_absolute() => p,
389	        _ => {
390	            let home = home.filter(|h| !h.is_empty())?;
391	            std::path::PathBuf::from(home).join(".config")
392	        }
393	    };
394	    Some(base.join("carapace").join("specs"))
395	}

397	/// Write the carapace spec to `dir/iiac-perf.yaml`, creating the
398	/// dir if needed and overwriting any existing spec; returns the
399	/// written path.
400	fn write_completion_yaml(dir: &std::path::Path) -> std::io::Result<std::path::PathBuf> {
401	    std::fs::create_dir_all(dir)?;
402	    let path = dir.join("iiac-perf.yaml");
403	    std::fs::write(&path, carapace_spec())?;
404	    Ok(path)
405	}

407	/// Inject dynamic bench-name completion into the generated carapace
408	/// spec: a `positionalany` list whose exec-macro asks the installed
409	/// binary (`--list-benches`) on every Tab, plus the two static
410	/// command words. The generator emits only what clap knows, so the
411	/// positional would otherwise complete to nothing.
412	fn inject_bench_candidates(spec: &str) -> String {
413	    let block = concat!(
414	        "completion:\n",
415	        "  positionalany:\n",
416	        "  - \"$(iiac-perf --list-benches)\"\n",
417	        "  - \"all\\trun every registered bench\"\n",
418	        "  - \"qualify-environment\\tis this machine fit to measure on?\"\n",
419	        "  - \"describe-record\\tprint the --record field dictionary\"\n",
420	        "  - \"add-completion-yaml\\twrite the carapace completion spec to the specs dir\"\n",
421	    );
422	    if spec.contains("completion:\n") {
423	        spec.replacen("completion:\n", block, 1)
424	    } else {
425	        format!("{spec}{block}")
426	    }
427	}

429	/// Wrap a name list into comma-separated lines of at most `width`
430	/// columns, each line indented two spaces — the no-benches
431	/// listing's counterpart of clap's two-column help style.
432	fn wrap_names(names: &[&str], width: usize) -> String {
433	    let mut out = String::new();
434	    let mut col = 0;
435	    for name in names {
436	        if out.is_empty() {
437	            out.push_str("  ");
438	        } else if col + 2 + name.len() <= width {
439	            out.push_str(", ");
440	        } else {
441	            out.push_str(",\n  ");
442	            col = 0;
443	        }
444	        out.push_str(name);
445	        col += 2 + name.len();
446	    }
447	    out
448	}

450	fn main() {
451	    let cli = Cli::parse();
452	
453	    // Completion generation and the bench-name listing are pure
454	    // print-and-exit paths: no logging, no config, no setup.
455	    if let Some(shell) = cli.completions {
456	        print_completions(shell);
457	        return;
458	    }
459	    if cli.list_benches {
460	        for name in benches::names() {
461	            println!("{name}");
462	        }
463	        return;
464	    }
465	
466	    // 'describe-record' is a pure print-and-exit command word: the
467	    // record's field dictionary, documenting outputs the way
468	    // --help documents inputs.
469	    if cli.benches.iter().any(|b| b == "describe-record") {
470	        if cli.benches.len() > 1 {
471	            eprintln!("error: 'describe-record' runs alone; drop the other bench args");
472	            std::process::exit(2);
473	        }
474	        println!("{ABOUT}\n");
475	        record::describe();
476	        return;
477	    }
478	
479	    // 'add-completion-yaml' is a command word like 'all':
480	    // self-install the carapace spec, print the path, and exit.
481	    if cli.benches.iter().any(|b| b == "add-completion-yaml") {
482	        if cli.benches.len() > 1 {
483	            eprintln!("error: 'add-completion-yaml' runs alone; drop the other bench args");
484	            std::process::exit(2);
485	        }
486	        let dir = match cli.completion_dir.clone().or_else(default_completion_dir) {
487	            Some(d) => d,
488	            None => {
489	                eprintln!(
490	                    "error: no specs dir ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME and $HOME unset); pass --completion-dir"
491	                );
492	                std::process::exit(2);
493	            }
494	        };
495	        match write_completion_yaml(&dir) {
496	            Ok(path) => println!("{}", path.display()),
497	            Err(e) => {
498	                eprintln!(
499	                    "error: writing {}: {e}",
500	                    dir.join("iiac-perf.yaml").display()
501	                );
502	                std::process::exit(1);
503	            }
504	        }
505	        return;
506	    }
507	
508	    // Default filter is `warn`; `-v` bumps to `debug`. `RUST_LOG`
509	    // (if set) always wins — so users can still do fine-grained
510	    // per-module filtering without fighting the flag.
511	    let mut builder = env_logger::Builder::from_default_env();
512	    if std::env::var_os("RUST_LOG").is_none() {
513	        builder.filter_level(if cli.verbose {
514	            log::LevelFilter::Debug
515	        } else {
516	            log::LevelFilter::Warn
517	        });
518	    }
519	    builder.format_timestamp(None).init();
520	
521	    if cli.benches.is_empty() {
522	        println!("{ABOUT}\n");
523	        println!("no benches specified. use -h or --help for more info.\n");
524	        println!("Benches:");
525	        println!("{}\n", wrap_names(&benches::names(), 72));
526	        println!("{COMMANDS_HELP}");
527	        // Nudge toward completion setup until the spec exists at
528	        // the default path; silent once installed (or if a custom
529	        // --completion-dir was used — only the default is checked).
530	        let spec_missing =
531	            default_completion_dir().is_some_and(|d| !d.join("iiac-perf.yaml").exists());
532	        if spec_missing {
533	            println!("\nFor command completion execute 'iiac-perf add-completion-yaml -h'");
534	        }
535	        return;
536	    }
537	
538	    // 'qualify-environment' is a command, not a bench: it respawns
539	    // --runs times and grades the box across those runs. It stands
540	    // alone, and it re-execs children itself, so it runs before
541	    // the inhibit/config/banner path a bench run needs.
542	    if cli.benches.iter().any(|b| b == "qualify-environment") {
543	        if cli.benches.len() > 1 {
544	            eprintln!("error: 'qualify-environment' runs alone; drop the other bench args");
545	            std::process::exit(2);
546	        }
547	        println!("{ABOUT}\n");
548	        let code = qualify::run(&qualify::QualifyCfg {
549	            runs: cli.runs,
550	            gap_s: cli.gap,
551	            duration_s: cli.duration.unwrap_or(QUALIFY_CHILD_SECONDS),
552	            pin: cli.pin.clone(),
553	            print_only: cli.print_only,
554	            settle_time: cli.settle_time,
555	        });
556	        std::process::exit(code);
557	    }
558	
559	    // Re-exec under systemd-inhibit (unless --no-inhibit or
560	    // already inhibited) before any output, so the banner prints
561	    // once, from the inhibited child.
562	    let inhibit_status = inhibit::ensure(cli.no_inhibit);
563	
564	    // Layered defaults (built-in < XDG file < project-local file <
565	    // CLI). A malformed config is fatal so a typo surfaces.
566	    let (config, config_files) = match config::load() {
567	        Ok(c) => c,
568	        Err(e) => {
569	            eprintln!("error: config: {e}");
570	            std::process::exit(2);
571	        }
572	    };
573	
574	    println!("{ABOUT}\n");
575	
576	    if let Some(mask) = pin::current_affinity() {
577	        info!("startup affinity: {}", pin::affinity_summary(&mask));
578	    }
579	
580	    let pin_cores: Vec<usize> = match cli.pin.as_deref() {
581	        None => Vec::new(),
582	        // A spec naming a config profile expands to its core list;
583	        // anything else parses as a raw core spec.
584	        Some(spec) => match pin::parse_cores(config.resolve_pin(spec)) {
585	            Ok(v) => v,
586	            Err(e) => {
587	                eprintln!("error: --pin: {e}");
588	                std::process::exit(2);
589	            }
590	        },
591	    };
592	
593	    // Pin main to the pool's first slot when --pin is given: thread 0 of a bench measures on
594	    // main, and the warm loop is a real timing phase converging on per-core frequency state, so
595	    // it must run where measurement will run. Without --pin, main stays wherever the scheduler
596	    // has it: a busy thread stays put, and the warm state lands on the core that measures. The
597	    // retired CPU0-default warm pin parked the warm on the kernel's busiest core for no
598	    // measured benefit: the tick-rate read is a ratio that cancels interruptions (~8e-7 spread
599	    // across cores), and nothing else ran pinned.
600	    if let Some(&cpu) = pin_cores.first() {
601	        pin::pin_current(Some(cpu));
602	        info!("pinned main to core {cpu} (bench pin pool slot 0)");
603	    }
604	    if let Some(mask) = pin::current_affinity() {
605	        debug!("affinity for warm + run: {}", pin::affinity_summary(&mask));
606	    }
607	
608	    // Warm the one-time TSC tick-rate calibration (a ~10 ms spin behind a OnceLock) here on
609	    // main. Without this the first TProbe::new in a bench thread pays it inside the measurement
610	    // window: a short -d (e.g. 0.01) was consumed entirely by that spin and recorded zero
611	    // samples.
612	    let ticks_per_ns = ticks::ticks_per_ns();
613	    debug!("ticks_per_ns: {ticks_per_ns:.6}");
614	
615	    // Same precedence as duration: CLI, then config, then the
616	    // built-in. Negative is rejected rather than clamped: it
617	    // means the caller expected something we don't do.
618	    let settle_time = cli
619	        .settle_time
620	        .or(config.settle_time)
621	        .unwrap_or(harness::DEFAULT_SETTLE_TIME_S);
622	    if settle_time < 0.0 {
623	        eprintln!("error: --settle-time must be zero or more, got {settle_time}");
624	        std::process::exit(2);
625	    }
626	
627	    // Same precedence as settle time: CLI, then config, then the built-in.
628	    let warm_cap = cli
629	        .warm_cap
630	        .or(config.warm_cap)
631	        .unwrap_or(harness::DEFAULT_WARM_CAP_S);
632	    if warm_cap < 0.0 {
633	        eprintln!("error: --warm-cap must be zero or more, got {warm_cap}");
634	        std::process::exit(2);
635	    }
636	
637	    // Main's placement covers the warm loop and thread 0 of every bench, so the cell names
638	    // both.
639	    let main_pin_display = match pin_cores.first() {
640	        Some(c) => format!("core {c} (pool slot 0; warm + run)"),
641	        None => "none (scheduler placement)".to_string(),
642	    };
643	    // The box's clock and power policy, printed before any bench so every archived report says
644	    // what machine produced it. No report before 0.25.0 recorded the policy, which left an 8.9%
645	    // governor delta indistinguishable from a code change in any A/B spanning one.
646	    let policy = freq::policy();
647	    let boost = policy.boost.as_ref().map(|f| freq::PolicyField {
648	        value: boost_word(&f.value).to_string(),
649	        uniform: f.uniform,
650	    });
651	    println!("Setup:");
652	    println!("  ticks/ns          {ticks_per_ns:.6}");
653	    println!("  tick period       {:.3} ns", 1.0 / ticks_per_ns);
654	    println!(
655	        "  cpufreq driver    {}",
656	        policy_cell(policy.driver.as_ref())
657	    );
658	    println!(
659	        "  governor          {}",
660	        policy_cell(policy.governor.as_ref())
661	    );
662	    println!("  EPP               {}", policy_cell(policy.epp.as_ref()));
663	    println!("  boost             {}", policy_cell(boost.as_ref()));
664	    println!("  main pin          {main_pin_display}");
665	    println!("  bench pin         {}", pin::plan_summary(&pin_cores));
666	    // The budgets, not the spend: each run's report brackets carry
667	    // its own warm=used/cap, and the grade block's settle cell says
668	    // when the box settled.
669	    println!("  warm budget       settle {settle_time}s once + cap {warm_cap}s per run");
670	    println!("  sleep inhibit     {inhibit_status}");
671	    println!("  config            {}", config_summary(&config_files));
672	    println!();
673	
674	    // The record sink resolves before any bench runs, so a bad
675	    // path or tag fails in milliseconds rather than after minutes
676	    // of measuring.
677	    let recorder = match cli.record.as_deref() {
678	        None => None,
679	        Some(path) => match record::Recorder::new(path, &cli.tag) {
680	            Ok(r) => Some(r),
681	            Err(e) => {
682	                eprintln!("error: --record: {e}");
683	                std::process::exit(2);
684	            }
685	        },
686	    };
687	
688	    let runners = match benches::resolve(&cli.benches) {
689	        Ok(r) => r,
690	        Err(e) => {
691	            eprintln!("error: {e}");
692	            std::process::exit(2);
693	        }
694	    };
695	
696	    // Duration precedence: CLI -d / -D win, then the config
697	    // `duration`, then the built-in default.
698	    let target_seconds = match (cli.duration, cli.total_duration) {
699	        (Some(d), _) => d,
700	        (None, Some(t)) => t / runners.len() as f64,
701	        (None, None) => config.duration.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_DURATION),
702	    };
703	
704	    let cfg = harness::RunCfg {
705	        target_seconds,
706	        outer_override: cli.outer,
707	        inner_override: cli.inner,
708	        pin_cores: &pin_cores,
709	        report_ticks: cli.ticks,
710	        seam_probes: !cli.no_env_probe,
711	        band_labels: cli
712	            .band_labels
713	            .or(config.band_labels)
714	            .unwrap_or(DEFAULT_BAND_LABELS),
715	        decimals: cli.decimals.or(config.decimals).unwrap_or(DEFAULT_DECIMALS) as usize,
716	        settle_time_s: settle_time,
717	        warm_cap_s: warm_cap,
718	        blocks: cli.blocks,
719	        record: recorder.as_ref(),
720	    };
721	
722	    for run in runners {
723	        run(&cfg);
724	    }
725	}
726	
727	/// Render one `Setup:` policy cell: the token, marked when CPUs disagree, or why it is absent.
728	///
729	/// - `None` prints `not exposed` and never a default. A box without the file has no such
730	///   policy, and inventing one is exactly what makes an archived number ambiguous.
731	/// - A non-uniform field carries `(mixed across CPUs)`: one CPU's token is not the box's policy
732	///   when the policy groups were set separately.
733	fn policy_cell(field: Option<&freq::PolicyField>) -> String {
734	    match field {
735	        None => "not exposed".to_string(),
736	        Some(f) if f.uniform => f.value.clone(),
737	        Some(f) => format!("{} (mixed across CPUs)", f.value),
738	    }
739	}
740	
741	/// `boost`'s raw sysfs token as a word; anything unrecognized passes through untranslated
742	/// rather than being guessed at.
743	fn boost_word(raw: &str) -> &str {
744	    match raw {
745	        "1" => "enabled",
746	        "0" => "disabled",
747	        other => other,
748	    }
749	}
750	
751	#[cfg(test)]
752	mod tests {
753	    use super::*;
754	
755	    fn policy_field(value: &str, uniform: bool) -> freq::PolicyField {
756	        freq::PolicyField {
757	            value: value.to_string(),
758	            uniform,
759	        }
760	    }
761	
762	    #[test]
763	    fn policy_cell_says_absent_rather_than_defaulting() {
764	        assert_eq!(policy_cell(None), "not exposed");
765	    }
766	
767	    #[test]
768	    fn policy_cell_marks_a_split_policy() {
769	        assert_eq!(
770	            policy_cell(Some(&policy_field("powersave", true))),
771	            "powersave"
772	        );
773	        assert_eq!(
774	            policy_cell(Some(&policy_field("powersave", false))),
775	            "powersave (mixed across CPUs)"
776	        );
777	    }
778	
779	    #[test]
780	    fn boost_word_translates_only_the_known_tokens() {
781	        assert_eq!(boost_word("1"), "enabled");
782	        assert_eq!(boost_word("0"), "disabled");
783	        assert_eq!(boost_word("unexpected"), "unexpected");
784	    }
785	
786	    #[test]
787	    fn wrap_names_single_line() {
788	        assert_eq!(wrap_names(&["a", "b"], 72), "  a, b");
789	    }
790	
791	    #[test]
792	    fn inject_bench_candidates_precedes_flag_section() {
793	        let spec = "name: x\ncompletion:\n  flag:\n    a:\n    - one\n";
794	        let out = inject_bench_candidates(spec);
795	        // positionalany lands under the existing completion key,
796	        // before the flag section; the exec-macro is quoted.
797	        let pos = out.find("  positionalany:").expect("positionalany missing");
798	        let flag = out.find("  flag:").expect("flag section missing");
799	        assert!(pos < flag);
800	        assert!(out.contains("\"$(iiac-perf --list-benches)\""));
801	        assert_eq!(out.matches("completion:\n").count(), 1);
802	    }
803	
804	    #[test]
805	    fn inject_bench_candidates_appends_when_no_completion_key() {
806	        let out = inject_bench_candidates("name: x\n");
807	        assert!(out.ends_with(
808	            "- \"add-completion-yaml\\twrite the carapace completion spec to the specs dir\"\n"
809	        ));
810	        assert!(out.contains("completion:\n  positionalany:\n"));
811	    }
812	
813	    #[test]
814	    fn completion_dir_prefers_absolute_xdg() {
815	        let dir = completion_dir_from(Some("/xdg".into()), Some("/home/u".into()));
816	        assert_eq!(dir, Some("/xdg/carapace/specs".into()));
817	    }
818	
819	    #[test]
820	    fn completion_dir_ignores_relative_xdg() {
821	        let dir = completion_dir_from(Some("rel".into()), Some("/home/u".into()));
822	        assert_eq!(dir, Some("/home/u/.config/carapace/specs".into()));
823	    }
824	
825	    #[test]
826	    fn completion_dir_none_without_home() {
827	        assert_eq!(completion_dir_from(None, None), None);
828	        assert_eq!(completion_dir_from(None, Some("".into())), None);
829	    }
830	
831	    #[test]
832	    fn wrap_names_breaks_at_width() {
833	        // "ccc" would land past col 10, so it wraps; the separator
834	        // comma stays on the prior line and the new line re-indents.
835	        assert_eq!(wrap_names(&["aaa", "bbb", "ccc"], 10), "  aaa, bbb,\n  ccc");
836	    }
837	}

1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
4	suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
5	copied **verbatim**, with
6	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
7	conditional rather than per-project edits.
8	
9	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
10	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
11	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
12	
13	## Terms
14	
15	Three names, used as defined here across
16	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
17	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
18	
19	- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
20	  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
21	  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
22	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
23	  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
24	  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
25	- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
26	  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
27	  artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## A stamp, not a name
31	
32	The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
33	named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
34	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
35	suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
36	inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.
37	
38	## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides
39	
40	Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
41	touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**
42	
43	- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
44	  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
45	  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
46	  presentation, docs, notes.
47	- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
48	  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
49	- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
50	  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).
51	
52	**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
53	thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.
54	
55	## Grammar and storage
56	
57	One spelling everywhere the version is written:
58	
59	```
60	<public>[-<suffix>]
61	```
62	
63	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
64	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
65	  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
66	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
67	  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
68	  version storable in every medium below.
69	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
70	  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability, while manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a
71	  leading `v`. Cargo rejects one.)
72	
73	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
74	
75	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
76	  valid at any dot depth.
77	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
78	  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
79	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
80	  adds its case to
81	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
82	
83	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
84	
85	- **The stored version identifies but does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
86	  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out), while PEP 440 sorts the
87	  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
88	  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
89	  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
90	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
91	  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
92	  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.
93	
94	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
95	multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
96	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
97	`+` are all invalid. `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth. `1.2.3-1` parses but
98	silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
99	every medium accepts.
100	
101	## Recording the version-of-record
102	
103	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
104	the case that fits your medium:
105	
106	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
107	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
108	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
109	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
110	    ...). Add the case as needed
111	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
112	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
113	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
114	    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
115	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
116	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
117	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
118	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
119	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
120	  per-commit preference.
121	
122	## Dev artifact name
123	
124	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
125	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
126	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
127	
128	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
129	  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
130	  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
131	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
132	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
133	  install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
135	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
136	  flow's install.
137	
138	Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
139	its `custom.md` layer.
140	
141	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
142	
143	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
144	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
145	
146	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
147	  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
148	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
149	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
150	  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
151	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
152	
153	## Suffix scheme
154	
155	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
156	each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157	
158	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159	not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160	neither a number nor a version (see
161	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162	prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163	commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164	nothing dereferences one.
165	
166	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
168	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169	
170	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
171	and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
172	Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
173	without renumbering siblings.
174	
175	Disambiguation:
176	
177	- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
178	- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
179	
180	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
181	
182	- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
183	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
184	- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
185	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
186	
187	Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
188	step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
189	above, every commit carries a distinct version.

  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides

Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**

- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
  presentation, docs, notes.
- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).

**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
  version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability, while manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a
  leading `v`. Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
  valid at any dot depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
  adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies but does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out), while PEP 440 sorts the
  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
`+` are all invalid. `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth. `1.2.3-1` parses but
silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

1	//! Explicit CPU-frequency control: the `read-freq` / `pin-freq` / `restore-freq` command words
2	//! and the `--pin-freq` run guard.
3	//!
4	//! [`crate::freq`] reads and never writes. This module is the one place the harness mutates the
5	//! box, and the reasons mutation used to be banned outright (root, global, persistent) survive
6	//! as its design constraints:
7	//!
8	//! - mutation happens only on an explicit command word or flag, never as a side effect
9	//! - a pinned run restores on every catchable exit path: normal return and panic via the
10	//!   guard's `Drop`, SIGINT and SIGTERM via a pre-rendered async-signal-safe handler
11	//! - restore converges to a steady state the user *declared* in the config's `[freq]` section,
12	//!   never to a remembered one. A remembered state ratchets on back-to-back runs (run 2
13	//!   "restores" run 1's pin), and transient state files are a demonstrated failure mode in this
14	//!   repo. Declared-state convergence is idempotent from any starting point, which is also the
15	//!   whole recovery story after SIGKILL or power loss: run `restore-freq`, nothing saved to
16	//!   find
17	//!
18	//! Writes are staged as ordered **plans** of (path, token) pairs because cpufreq rejects
19	//! `min > max`: every clamp move goes floor-first (min to the hardware floor, then max, then
20	//! min), so each intermediate write is valid from any starting state. A pin is `min = max` at
21	//! the target with boost off, and the load-independent default target is the base clock
22	//! ([`freq::base_clock`]), the manufacturer's guaranteed all-core sustained frequency.
23	
24	use std::ffi::CString;
25	use std::sync::OnceLock;
26	
27	use crate::config::FreqConfig;
28	use crate::freq;
29	
30	/// An ordered list of sysfs writes: (absolute path, token). Order is load-bearing, see the
31	/// module doc's floor-first rule.
32	type Plan = Vec<(String, String)>;
33	
34	/// The kernel's single boost knob when the driver has no per-CPU `boost` files.
35	const GLOBAL_BOOST: &str = "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost";
36	
37	/// Path of one per-CPU cpufreq knob.
38	fn knob(cpu: usize, name: &str) -> String {
39	    format!("/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu{cpu}/cpufreq/{name}")
40	}
41	
42	/// Which boost control the box exposes, decided once at capability read.
43	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
44	enum BoostKnob {
45	    /// No boost control at all (rpi5-20cd).
46	    None,
47	    /// Per-CPU `cpufreq/boost` files.
48	    PerCpu,
49	    /// The single global `cpufreq/boost` file.
50	    Global,
51	}
52	
53	/// One CPU's write targets and validation data.
54	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
55	struct CpuCaps {
56	    /// The logical CPU number.
57	    cpu: usize,
58	    /// `cpuinfo_min_freq` (kHz): the hardware floor, and the staging value for clamp moves.
59	    hw_min_khz: u64,
60	    /// `cpuinfo_max_freq` (kHz): the hardware ceiling.
61	    hw_max_khz: u64,
62	    /// Discrete `scaling_available_frequencies` (kHz) where the driver lists them, `None` on
63	    /// continuous-range drivers (amd-pstate, intel_pstate).
64	    avail_khz: Option<Vec<u64>>,
65	}
66	
67	/// What the box exposes, read once per command: write targets plus the data that validates a
68	/// declared state against reality.
69	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
70	struct BoxCaps {
71	    /// Per-CPU capabilities, ascending by CPU.
72	    cpus: Vec<CpuCaps>,
73	    /// Whether `energy_performance_preference` exists (amd-pstate-epp yes, rpi5-20cd no).
74	    has_epp: bool,
75	    /// `scaling_available_governors`, when readable, for validating the declared governor.
76	    governors: Option<Vec<String>>,
77	    /// `energy_performance_available_preferences`, when readable.
78	    epp_prefs: Option<Vec<String>>,
79	    /// Which boost control exists.
80	    boost: BoostKnob,
81	}
82	
83	/// Read the box's capabilities from sysfs. Errors when there is no cpufreq to control (a VM,
84	/// typically), naming what is missing.
85	fn read_caps() -> Result<BoxCaps, String> {
86	    let cpu_ids = freq::cpus();
87	    let Some(&first) = cpu_ids.first() else {
88	        return Err("no CPUs under /sys/devices/system/cpu".to_string());
89	    };
90	    let mut cpus = Vec::with_capacity(cpu_ids.len());
91	    for cpu in cpu_ids {
92	        let (Some(hw_min_khz), Some(hw_max_khz)) = (
93	            freq::read_khz(cpu, "cpuinfo_min_freq"),
94	            freq::read_khz(cpu, "cpuinfo_max_freq"),
95	        ) else {
96	            return Err(format!(
97	                "cpu{cpu} exposes no cpufreq range (cpuinfo_min_freq/cpuinfo_max_freq): \
98	                 nothing to control"
99	            ));
100	        };
101	        cpus.push(CpuCaps {
102	            cpu,
103	            hw_min_khz,
104	            hw_max_khz,
105	            avail_khz: freq::available_khz(cpu),
106	        });
107	    }
108	    let boost = if freq::read_token(first, "boost").is_some() {
109	        BoostKnob::PerCpu
110	    } else if std::path::Path::new(GLOBAL_BOOST).exists() {
111	        BoostKnob::Global
112	    } else {
113	        BoostKnob::None
114	    };
115	    Ok(BoxCaps {
116	        cpus,
117	        has_epp: freq::read_token(first, "energy_performance_preference").is_some(),
118	        governors: token_list(first, "scaling_available_governors"),
119	        epp_prefs: token_list(first, "energy_performance_available_preferences"),
120	        boost,
121	    })
122	}
123	
124	/// One whitespace-separated token-list file for `cpu`, `None` when absent.
125	fn token_list(cpu: usize, name: &str) -> Option<Vec<String>> {
126	    let text = freq::read_token(cpu, name)?;
127	    Some(text.split_whitespace().map(str::to_string).collect())
128	}
129	
130	/// The declared steady state, validated against the box: what `restore-freq` converges to.
131	#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
132	struct Steady {
133	    /// The declared governor token.
134	    governor: String,
135	    /// The declared EPP token, present exactly when the box has EPP.
136	    epp: Option<String>,
137	    /// The declared boost switch, present exactly when the box has a boost knob.
138	    boost: Option<bool>,
139	    /// Declared lower clamp (kHz), `None` meaning each CPU's hardware floor.

141	    /// Declared upper clamp (kHz), `None` meaning each CPU's hardware ceiling.
142	    max_khz: Option<u64>,
143	}

content.text: Per-commit checklist step 3: complete the ladder details and flip the rung. Reading prose.md first, as it governs durable text:

content.content:
1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
8	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
14	or the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
15	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
16	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One
17	fact per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs:
18	they hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without
19	naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See
20	[Semicolons](#semicolons) and
21	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
22	
23	Surfaces that use this shape:
24	
25	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See
26	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
27	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The title is the commit-specific
28	  add-on. See [Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
29	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`. See
30	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
31	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners
32	  are still fine. Done entries take the same shape with the title bolded, detail always as
33	  sub-bullets rather than sentences trailing off the title line. See
34	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form).
35	
36	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
37	
38	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged
39	  by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
40	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader
41	    meets first and it answers the problem
42	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them
43	    is a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
44	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A
45	    bullet wanting a paragraph belongs in the chores section instead
46	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
47	    live in the chores section, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names,
48	    each reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs
49	    here
50	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
51	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
52	  list. See
53	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
54	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
55	
56	### Line widths
57	
58	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather
59	than restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated
60	2026-08-09, when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
61	
62	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
63	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
64	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
65	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
66	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
67	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
68	
69	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps
70	when touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than
71	imitating the narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL,
72	a literal report row, indented code in a comment).
73	
74	### Problem-first shape
75	
76	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores sections, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper
77	form of the same shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
78	
79	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate
80	  what follows it.
81	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms,
82	  answering whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in
83	  [Bullet content differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
84	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
85	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See
86	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
87	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
88	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is
89	    picked up into a cycle.
90	
91	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A
92	cycle writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's
93	commit body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a
94	commit body's is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule
95	here said a plan was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle
96	unable to say at its opening what it intended to do.
97	
98	### Commit-body form
99	
100	A commit body is the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
101	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
102	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a
103	solution statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and
104	separately.
105	
106	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It
107	  is mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is
108	  a body a `--body` flag can mistake for an option.
109	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general
110	  problem, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is
111	  usually asking to be more than one commit.
112	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and a `-` solves the nearest enclosing problem: nested under a
113	  `*` facet it solves that facet, at top level it solves the intro's general problem, which is
114	  how one solution says it retires every facet at once. Position expresses scope.
115	- **Zero facets is the trivial commit**: a problem paragraph and one or more top-level `-`
116	  solutions. Not a second form, the general form with an empty middle.
117	
118	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution.
119	Indentation alone cannot separate them in the trivial case, where a lone top-level `-` reads as a
120	solution only because `-` always is one. The typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds
121	every facet, `^- ` and `^  - ` every solution). Bodies are read as plain text, in `jj log` and in
122	terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever flattens them the indentation still
123	carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and a linter's consistent-marker rule
124	is wrong to normalize them.
125	
126	Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
127	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
128	
129	### Semicolons
130	
131	Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
132	files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is
133	written explicitly instead:
134	
135	- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
136	  history keeps the record.").
137	- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
138	  onward rather than making its own claim.
139	- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so
140	  the structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather
141	  than separating with semicolons.
142	
143	The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code
144	first, then expects zero.
145	
146	The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are
147	swept to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is altered:
148	altering one is the moment to ask the user whether its semicolons should be removed, always,
149	never a license to convert or keep them silently.
150	
151	### Typeable punctuation only
152	
153	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on
154	*authoring*, not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see
155	below), so a byte scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment.
156	Banned from authoring: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a
157	paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag.
158	Like the semicolon rule above this one is absolute, and stricter with history: no ask-on-alter,
159	no exemption at all, because a banned character costs nothing to write and is paid on every
160	read, so a soft rule accumulates them.
161	
162	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
163	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
164	
165	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
166	  sub-bullets.
167	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
168	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
169	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
170	  go.
171	
172	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
173	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
174	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
175	commit.
176	
177	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
178	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
179	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
180	prose. It applies going forward, and existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
181	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
182	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
183	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
184	
185	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
186	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
187	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
188	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
189	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
190	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
191	
192	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
193	
194	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
195	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
196	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
197	They differ in the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the
198	[Commit-body form](#commit-body-form), ladder / chores are conceptual (see "Bullet *content*
199	differs by surface" above). The shared template:
200	
201	```
202	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
203	<optional prose intro>
204	  - <optional item>
205	    <optional prose intro>
206	      - <optional sub-item>
207	      ...
208	```
209	
210	The three surfaces apply it as:
211	
212	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is
213	  `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)`: the as-built `[[N]]` placeholder carried from birth, the
214	  title reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's
215	  `# References` (the closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker.
216	  Its position in the list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its
217	  text says so. Detail lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection
218	  headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
219	  [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
220	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no prefix, since the `##` header *is* the
221	  bare title. The as-built ladder is the first content under it (see
222	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
223	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose
224	  (see [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description)).
225	
226	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
227	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection
228	heading carries the same title, a fourth surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only
229	when close-out gotchas occurred: see the protocol's
230	[Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
231	
232	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
233	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
234	section header carries the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the
235	bookends below). To keep a cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the
236	step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
237	
238	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a
239	suffix, " opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
240	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
241	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the chores `##` header and
242	the `## Done` entry carry it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the
243	closing rung's subsection anchor clear of the section header's. A single-step cycle's one
244	commit is the cycle and keeps the bare title. The type repeats across the pair even though the
245	bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make them scannable. Rungs between keep
246	their own titles on the stem.
247	
248	### Steps are named, not numbered
249	
250	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung, a chores as-built rung, a `## Done`
251	entry, or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a rung's place in the list already *is* its place in
252	the ladder, so a number beside it would restate the position and then have to be maintained.
253	
254	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
255	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
256	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable in the two places a
257	  title is resolved: within its own cycle, so a ladder rung names one step, and within its chores
258	  file, since a `##` header is also an anchor and a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first
259	  one. Across the repo's history a title may repeat.
260	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and
261	  nothing else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder
262	  come along. See
263	  [Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
264	- **`## Todo` ranks are the exception that stays numbered**, because a priority list has an order
265	  worth reading off (see [Todo format](notes.md#todo-format)). Those numbers are positional too,
266	  and are equally never used as references.
267	
268	### Versions live in the version-of-record only
269	
270	No version appears in durable prose: not in an in-flight ladder rung, a chores header, a commit
271	title, or a commit body. The manifest is the version's only written home (see
272	[versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's version is read from that file at that
273	commit.
274	
275	**Why:** the version is a build stamp answering "which commit produced this artifact", not a name
276	for a step. Written into prose it becomes a second identifier that history is free to invalidate:
277	one renumber of published versions turns every prose mention, transcript and pasted report into
278	residue that needs a decoder to read. A renumber cannot touch a title.
279	
280	**Two surfaces record a version rather than name a step.** Both record a *commit*, never a step,
281	which is what keeps them outside the rule rather than exceptions to it:
282	
283	- **A chores as-built rung** records a version alongside that commit's SHA once the commit is on
284	  a permanent branch. The pair decodes an old `-V` banner or a pasted report. It obeys the SHA's
285	  timing exactly, so a rung on an unlanded branch carries neither (see
286	  [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
287	- **A `## Done` entry**, in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`, carries the close-out's version ahead of
288	  its title (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Here the version is the search
289	  key: the question a reader arrives with is "what shipped in 0.42.0", and with no version
290	  written anywhere in the Done list that question has no answer.
291	
292	The two differ in timing, and the reason is the SHA rather than the version. The rung waits
293	because a commit cannot record its own SHA. A Done entry has no SHA to wait for and its version
294	is already in the manifest of the commit it is written in, so it is written at close-out. On an
295	unlanded bookmark it is a draft like the rest of the line
296	([Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)), and a renumber of
297	published versions rewrites it in the same sweep as the rungs.
298	
299	**How to apply:** name the step by its title and the phase in words ("the close-out", "the
300	opening"). Writing *about* versioning is unaffected: a version named as a specimen, whether in the
301	scheme's own notation, a decoder table, or a narrative about a renumber, is a use of the word
302	rather than an identifier for a step, the same distinction
303	[Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only) draws between naming a character and using
304	one. Existing versioned prose is grandfathered and converts when touched, no sweep.
305	
306	## Pinned files name no project
307	
308	A pinned agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names a member project, a member's
309	history, or a member's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every member
310	shares and stay. What is barred is a member repo appearing in universal text.
311	
312	**Why:** pinned text is copied to every member, so a project narration reads as the reader's own
313	history ("This project adopted the convention on <date>" arrives in repos that adopted it on a
314	different date or never). And the citation goes stale the moment the named project retires its
315	records, while the rule outlives it.
316	
317	**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the pinned file, and leave the evidence trail
318	in the records of the project that earned it (chores, dogfood log), reachable from the commit
319	that changed the pinned file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not a member. A
320	specimen in
321	the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
322	reference, per the same distinction
323	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
324	draws.
325	
326	## Speculation marker
327	
328	Durable text the bot writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
329	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
330	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
331	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
332	
333	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
334	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
335	worth keeping visible in the written record.
336	
337	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
338	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
339	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
340	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
341	on hand.
342	
343	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
344	
345	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
346	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
347	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
348	
349	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread, and the plain form catches
350	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
351	
352	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
353	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
354	synopsis.
355
